we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The pop-ups are short sentences that give me the exact numbers each question asks for (people, enslaved, House seats, senators, seats if counted in full or not at all). The blue and orange-red pies match the sheet and the legend, and Virginia's pie is clearly the biggest.

findings.where: q1-virginia view, Population in 1790 pop-up, first line; Q1 'Who lived where in 1790?' step 3
findings.what: The first line says '(39.099998474121094%)'. That's a giant number. Do I copy all of it? I have to do this for every state to see which ones are more than a quarter.
findings.why: Jordan has to compare each state's percentage with 'a quarter'. A 16-digit decimal is hard to read and copy, and he may not see that it just means about 39%. Doing it for 15 states makes him want to quit.
findings.suggestion: Round the percentage in the pop-up to a whole number (e.g. 'about 39%'), with Round() in the pop-up's Arcade or the field's number format set to 0 decimal places.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png; pop-up text '292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%)'

findings.where: q1-virginia and q2-seats views, Population in 1790 pop-up; Q3 'The three-fifths clause' step 2
findings.what: The sheet says read 'the last two lines'. I scroll to the bottom and the last lines are about Kentucky and 'Seats: National Archives'. The 22 and the 13 are in the middle, not at the end.
findings.why: Jordan follows steps word for word. The box is cut off and has to scroll, so the real last lines are out of sight, and they're the wrong ones. He may leave the 'if counted in full / not at all' blanks empty or fill them with the wrong numbers.
findings.suggestion: Change step 2 to 'then read the line that starts If enslaved people had been counted in full' (it is the third paragraph), or move that sentence to the end of the pop-up, after the Kentucky/Maine note.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png (box cut off at 'West Virginia as part'); pop-up order: census line, three-fifths line, 'If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.', note about Kentucky and outlines, 'Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'

findings.where: q2-seats view, House seats in 1793 labels mixed with Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels; Q2 'Seats in Congress' step 2
findings.what: I see 'NY: 10' and also 'NY 11'. There's 'VT 14', 'RI 13', 'NC 12', 'SC 8', and 'GA 4' next to 'GA: 2'. Does Vermont have 14 seats? Which New York number is the seats?
findings.why: In this picture the ratification pies and their order labels are drawn on top of the seats map. They look almost the same as the seats labels (only the colon is different), so Jordan could write Vermont or Rhode Island as having lots of seats and get 'most' and 'fewest' wrong.
findings.suggestion: Check that Ratifying the Constitution really stays off until Q4: the legend for this view lists only House seats in 1793 and Population, but the ratification pies and labels are drawn. Also make the two kinds of label look different, e.g. 'VT 14th' for ratification order and 'NY 10 seats' for seats.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png (labels 'NH 9', 'VT 14', 'NY 11', 'RI 13', 'PA 2', 'MD 7', 'VA 10', 'NC (1788)', 'NC 12', 'GA 4', 'SC 8' beside 'NY: 10', 'PA: 13', 'VA: 19', 'CT: 7', 'NC: 10', 'GA: 2', 'KY: 2'); legend text for this view lists only House seats in 1793 and Population in 1790

findings.where: q2-seats view, House seats in 1793 labels; Q2 answer 'which the fewest?'
findings.what: Only seven states have a seats number I can read: NY 10, PA 13, VA 19, NC 10, CT 7, KY 2, GA 2. Delaware, Rhode Island, New Jersey, Maryland, Massachusetts and the rest have none, so I'd say Kentucky or Georgia had the fewest.
findings.why: Labels get squeezed out in the smallest states, and those are the states the 'fewest' question is about. I think Delaware had 1 seat (I'd check that against the 1793 apportionment). The lightest legend class is '1 to 2 seats', so the colour can't tell 1 from 2 either.
findings.suggestion: Let every seats label draw (turn off label overlap checks for this layer, or use smaller text or offshore labels with leader lines for DE, RI, NJ and MD), and give 1 seat its own legend class. The sheet could also send students to the New England and New York bookmark to read the small states.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png; legend text '13 to 19 seats / 7 to 10 seats / 4 to 6 seats / 1 to 2 seats'

findings.where: q4-ratify view, Ratifying the Constitution labels along the Virginia and Carolina coast; Q4 steps 3-4
findings.what: The 'NC (1788)' label is touching a pie that's half blue and half orange. 'NC 12' is next to a pie that's mostly orange, so did North Carolina vote no when it said yes? 'VA 10' is next to a different pie too.
findings.why: Each label sits up and to the right of its own pie, so on the crowded coast it lands on the next pie. In this view the pie beside 'NC 12' looks like the 1788 Hillsborough vote, the half-and-half pie beside 'NC (1788)' looks like Virginia, and the pie above 'VA 10' looks like Maryland. Jordan will match labels to the wrong pies unless he reads every pop-up title carefully.
findings.suggestion: Put each label directly under or on its own pie (or make the pies smaller), then check the Virginia, Maryland and both North Carolina pies in this view.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png

findings.where: q4-ratify view, northern pies (New York and New England); Q4 step 3
findings.what: The pies at the top are piled on top of each other. I can't click the one I want, and some of them have no label at all.
findings.why: To find the three closest votes Jordan has to read every pie's pop-up, and several close votes are in that pile. Labels for Delaware, New Jersey, Connecticut and Massachusetts don't show in this view.
findings.suggestion: Add a step to Q4: 'Open the New England and New York bookmark to click the northern pies' (the bookmark is already in the app), or shrink the pie size range for this layer.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png

findings.where: q4-nc view, Ratifying the Constitution pop-up, first line; Q4 step 3
findings.what: 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM'. Why does it say midnight? Is that part of the answer?
findings.why: The time means nothing and adds one more thing to puzzle over in the very line he's told to read.
findings.suggestion: Show the date as '21 November 1789' with no time (a date-only format in the pop-up).
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png; pop-up text 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM: 194 for, 77 against.'

findings.where: Map layers list, House seats today (2020 apportionment) just above House seats in 1793; Q2 step 1
findings.what: There are two 'House seats' layers. I might turn on 'House seats today' because it comes first.
findings.why: The sheet never uses the 2020 layer. If Jordan turns it on he reads modern numbers and his Q2 answers are wrong.
findings.suggestion: Remove the 2020 layer from this map, or rename it so it can't be mistaken (e.g. 'Extra: seats in 2020') and move it to the bottom of the list.
findings.evidence: Map layers list: 'House seats today (2020 apportionment) (off)' above 'House seats in 1793 (off)'

findings.where: open and q2-seats views, legend headings; Q1 and Q2
findings.what: The legend says 'Total1790' and 'HouseSeats'. Those look like computer words.
findings.why: Small, but it's another word that trips him up in the legend the sheet points him to.
findings.suggestion: Rename the size heading to 'People in 1790' and the seats heading to 'House seats' in each layer's legend settings.
findings.evidence: Legend text 'Total1790' and 'HouseSeats'; we-the-people-1787-1791--open.png

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: The district pop-up is one plain sentence, 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15', so Q1 is quick once I find my town. The historic-place pop-up puts the place's name in bold at the top.

findings.where: open view, whole map; Q1 'Who represents us?' step 1
findings.what: The map starts on all of North America. I have to zoom and drag a lot to get to my town, and there's no box to type my town in.
findings.why: Jordan gives up when a step drags on. Every later question starts from his town, so a slow start eats the lesson time.
findings.suggestion: Add the Search tool to the app so students can type their town or school, or open the map zoomed to the school's state.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; tools listed: Basemaps, Map layers, Legend, Measure, Sketch, 2D/3D, Bookmarks (no search); the only bookmark is 'The United States'

findings.where: open and q1-district views, Congressional districts layer; Q1 step 4 and answer 'How many districts does your state have?'
findings.what: To get the number of districts I have to count little shapes. The state border is the same blue line as the district lines, so I can't tell where my state stops.
findings.why: Counting outlines by eye is slow and easy to get wrong in a big state, and nothing on the map gives the total.
findings.suggestion: Add the state's total to the pop-up ('Ohio has 15 districts'), or draw state borders in a thicker or different line.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; pop-up text 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'

findings.where: q4-nrhp and q4-nrhp-click views, National Register of Historic Places; Q4 'History where we live' step 3 (and 'Reading the map')
findings.what: The sheet says the pop-up has no name and tells me to read the label under the diamond. But there's no label under the diamonds, just street names. The pop-up has 'Ohio Statehouse' in bold at the top. Is that the name?
findings.why: The sheet and the map disagree, so Jordan doesn't trust what he sees and goes looking for a label that isn't there.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet to say the name is the bold title at the top of the pop-up, and drop the step about the basemap label and the archive link.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (no building names near the diamonds); pop-up title 'Ohio Statehouse'

findings.where: q4-nrhp view (the closest zoom pictured), Topographic basemap; Q2 'Rights in public places' steps 1-2
findings.what: I zoomed in until I can read every street and park name, but I don't see any courthouse, city hall or library names. How much more do I zoom?
findings.why: The question depends on building names, and he'll stop zooming once the map already looks zoomed in. Even the Ohio Statehouse grounds have no label at this zoom.
findings.suggestion: Check at which zoom the basemap starts naming public buildings and put that on the sheet ('zoom in until you can see single buildings, about N more clicks on +').
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png

findings.where: q4-nrhp-click view, National Register pop-up; Q4 step 2
findings.what: 'Property ID: 72001011' and then 'National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number: 72001011'. The same number twice, and long words I don't need.
findings.why: The extra lines make the box scroll, and the long words make him think he has to understand them.
findings.suggestion: Hide the Property ID and reference number fields in the pop-up; keep the name, address and 'Type: building'.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'Property ID: 72001011 ... National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number: 72001011'

findings.where: q4-nrhp-click view, highlighted Ohio Statehouse diamond; Q4 steps 2-3 and the pins in Q2
findings.what: The pop-up says the Statehouse is at High and Broad, but the diamond that lights up is down by the freeway near the Brewery District. If I pin the diamond, my pin is in the wrong place.
findings.why: If the diamonds don't sit on their buildings, reading the map under them (as the sheet says) gives the wrong place.
findings.suggestion: I'd check this point's location against its address (SE corner of High and Broad, which looks like the green block just below the 'Columbus' label in q4-nrhp). If points are often off, tell students to go by the pop-up address, not the diamond's spot.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png and rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png; pop-up text 'SE corner of High and Broad Sts.'

findings.where: q4-nrhp view, National Register legend colours; Q4 step 4
findings.what: The light yellow 'structure' and pale green 'object' diamonds are hard to see on the light map, and 'district' and 'site' are both reddish. What's the difference between a building, a structure and an object anyway?
findings.why: The diamonds are small and two pairs of colours are close. The pop-up already says 'Resource Type: building', which is easier than the legend.
findings.suggestion: Darken the pale colours and make the diamonds a bit bigger; on the sheet, point to the pop-up's 'Resource Type' line as well as the legend.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (legend); pop-up text 'Resource Type: building'

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: The 1796 pies are clean: solid orange or blue, with thin slivers that show which states split, and the pop-up title gives the state and its electors in a few words. Zoomed in, the two court squares are clearly labelled and the McCulloch 'Why here' is one plain sentence.

findings.where: q4-marbury view, Landmark Supreme Court cases, Marbury v. Madison square; Q4 'The Supreme Court, near the capital' steps 1-2
findings.what: I click the Marbury v. Madison square and nothing opens. I can't read its Why here.
findings.why: Half of the Q4 answer ('What happened in each place...') comes from this pop-up. With nothing to read, Jordan can't answer and is likely to stop there.
findings.suggestion: Check that pop-ups are turned on for the Marbury feature (and that the square, not just its label, is the clickable feature), then test the click at both the bookmark zoom and zoomed in.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png; pop-up text '(no pop-up opened)'

findings.where: open and q1-pie views (The sixteen states), Supreme Court squares on top of the Maryland pie; Q1 step 3, Q2 step 3 and 'Which state was the closest?'
findings.what: Two pink squares sit on top of one pie in the middle. I can't see its colours, and when I click it I get a court case.
findings.why: That pie is Maryland, which split its votes in 1796 and, I believe, split 5-5 in 1800 (I'd check), which would make it the answer to 'which state was the closest'. Jordan is likely to miss it.
findings.suggestion: Have the court cases layer off when the map opens and turn it on in Q4 (add that step to the sheet), or make it draw only when zoomed in closer than the bookmark.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png; presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png

findings.where: q2-1800 view, Election of 1800 pies; Q2 step 2 and Q3 'Which states switched?' step 2
findings.what: New York's pie is a dark green colour that's not in the legend. Pennsylvania's has three colours. Which one is Jefferson?
findings.why: New York is the state Q3 is about: its whole pie should change from orange to blue. If it shows a colour that isn't in the legend, Jordan can't answer.
findings.suggestion: Check whether the 1796 and 1800 pies are being drawn half see-through on top of each other (the olive green is what orange and blue make mixed half and half). Set both layers to full opacity with no blending, and check that turning 1796 off removes it. If this was only the fade while switching layers, no change is needed.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (New York pie olive green; Pennsylvania pie blue, green and yellow)

findings.where: q2-1800 view, pop-up left open from 1796; Q2 step 3 and Q3
findings.what: I turned on 1800 and the box still says 'Pennsylvania: 15 electors'. I'd copy those numbers for 1800, but they're from 1796.
findings.why: Both years' pop-ups have the same title, so the only clue to the year is inside the first line, and that's easy to miss.
findings.suggestion: Put the year in each pop-up title ('Pennsylvania in 1800: 15 electors'), and add 'close any open pop-up' to Q2 step 1.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png; pop-up text 'Pennsylvania: 15 electors / Electors' votes in 1796: ...'

findings.where: q1-pie view, 1796 pop-up; Q1 step 3 and 'Which states split their votes, and how?'
findings.what: It says Adams 1, Jefferson 14, Pinckney 2, Burr 13, but the pie only has two colours. Then it says 'Adams, 1 votes'.
findings.why: The numbers he needs (Adams and Jefferson) are mixed in with two other names, and the pie numbers come after a hard sentence about each elector casting two votes.
findings.suggestion: Start the pop-up with the pie numbers ('In the pie: Adams 1 vote, Jefferson 14 votes'), then list the other candidates, and fix '1 votes'.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14, Thomas Pinckney 2, Aaron Burr 13.' and 'John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes'

findings.where: open view, the two pink squares; Q4 steps 1 and 3
findings.what: At the start the two squares are on top of each other, so I can't click each one or measure between them.
findings.why: The sheet doesn't say to zoom in. Zoomed in, the squares are well apart and easy to click and measure.
findings.suggestion: Add 'Zoom in on the pink squares near the capital' to Q4 step 1, or add a bookmark for that zoomed view.

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: The yellow Louisiana Purchase, the trail and the campsites stand out, the purchase pop-up gives acres and price in one sentence, and the watershed pop-up name ('Missouri Region') is big and plain. At the Across the Rockies bookmark it's easy to see the trail leave the yellow and carry on to the coast.

findings.where: q1-purchase and q2-missouri-basin views, selection highlight on Territorial acquisitions and Watersheds; Q1 steps 2-3 and Q2
findings.what: When I click the yellow land it turns bright green. The sheet says green is the 1783 land. So which one is green now? The 1783 land looks more gray-blue to me.
findings.why: Q1 is a colour comparison, and the click the sheet asks for changes the colours. The 1783 land is a grayish teal, so 'green' already doesn't quite fit.
findings.suggestion: Change the app's highlight to an outline only, in a colour not used on the map, and call the 1783 land 'gray-green' on the sheet (or recolour it a clearer green).
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-missouri-basin.png

findings.where: open view with the legend open; Q1 step 2 and Q4 step 3
findings.what: With the legend open, the box covers most of the 1783 land and the east end of the trail.
findings.why: He needs both areas side by side to say how much bigger the country got.
findings.suggestion: Move The Louisiana Purchase bookmark so the 1783 land sits left of the legend panel (or zoom out a step), or add 'close the legend' to step 2.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png

findings.where: Territorial acquisitions, the 1783 land's pop-up (not pictured); Q1 answer 'About how much bigger did the country become?'
findings.what: The pop-up tells me how big the Louisiana Purchase is, but how big was the country before? I can only guess by looking.
findings.why: Without a number for the 1783 land, 'how much bigger' is a guess. I didn't see the 1783 pop-up, so it may already give one.
findings.suggestion: If the 1783 land's pop-up doesn't give its size, add it in acres so students can compare two numbers.
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'The Louisiana Purchase encompassed 530,000,000 acres of territory in North America that the United States purchased from France in 1803 for $15 million.'

findings.where: q1-purchase view, Louisiana Purchase pop-up; Q1 blank 'Size: about ___ million acres'
findings.what: The pop-up says '530,000,000 acres' but the sheet wants 'million acres'. How many millions is that? And what does 'encompassed' mean?
findings.why: Changing 530,000,000 into '530 million' is an extra step he may not see, and 'encompassed' is a word that stops him.
findings.suggestion: Reword the pop-up: 'The Louisiana Purchase was about 530 million acres (530,000,000). The United States bought it from France in 1803 for $15 million.'
findings.evidence: Pop-up text 'The Louisiana Purchase encompassed 530,000,000 acres of territory ...'

findings.where: q2-watersheds and q2-missouri-basin views, United States Watersheds; Q2 'Why New Orleans?' steps 2-3
findings.what: Which brown outline is 'along the Ohio River'? None of the rivers has a name. When I follow the rivers to the end there's no city name either, so I can't tell which city is at the mouth.
findings.why: The map has no place names, so the question depends on him already knowing the Ohio, the Mississippi and New Orleans. The trail runs along both rivers, but the sheet doesn't say so.
findings.suggestion: Add labels for the Ohio, Missouri and Mississippi rivers and a labelled New Orleans point; or add to the sheet 'the trail runs along both rivers' and 'click the outline where the rivers meet to read its name'.

findings.where: q2-watersheds legend and q2-missouri-basin pop-up; Q2 step 2
findings.what: 'Hydrologic Unit Code 2s' and 'HUC ID: 10'. What are those?
findings.why: Hard words at the top of the legend and the pop-up; the useful part is just 'Missouri Region'.
findings.suggestion: Rename the sublayer in the legend to 'Large river regions' and hide the HUC ID line in the pop-up.
findings.evidence: Legend text 'Hydrologic Unit Code 2s'; pop-up text 'Missouri Region / HUC ID: 10'

findings.where: q3-biomes view (Up the Missouri bookmark, Biomes on); Q3 'Up the Missouri' steps 3-4
findings.what: I turned on Biomes but nothing changed, it's still the same yellow. When I click, the first pop-up is 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region', not a biome.

findings.what: After the biome name it says 'Realm: Nearctic', 'Ecoregion', 'Nature Could Recover' and 'Half Protected'. I don't know those words.

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: The battle diamonds are easy to read: colour shows who won and size shows casualties, and the top of each pop-up gives the place, date, winner and casualties in three short lines. The treaty-line and recognition pop-ups are one or two plain sentences with exactly the fact the question asks for.

findings.where: q3-boundary view (The 1819 boundary bookmark, legend open), Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams-Onís Treaty line; Q3 steps 3-4
findings.what: I turned both layers on but the only green I see is a tiny patch in the mountains. Where's Florida? The legend box is on top of it, and the pink line runs under the box too.
findings.why: Jordan will click the tiny patch and think that's what Spain gave up. The Sabine and Red River parts of the line are also behind the legend, so he can't click all seven parts.
findings.suggestion: Move The 1819 boundary bookmark east or zoom out a step so Florida and the Sabine River sit left of the legend panel, or add 'close the legend' to step 2.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-boundary.png

findings.where: q3-treatyline view, Adams-Onís Treaty line part 1 (Sabine River); Q3 step 4
findings.what: Part 1 is a tiny bit of line right next to the big New Orleans diamond. I might click the battle instead. And I have to hit seven thin dashed lines.
findings.why: Clicking a thin line exactly is fiddly on a Chromebook trackpad, and it's easy to lose track of which parts he's done.
findings.suggestion: Make the treaty line thicker, put a small number label (1 to 7) on each part, and turn Battles off for Q3 (add that to step 2).
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-treatyline.png; pop-up text 'Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (part 1) / The Sabine River, from the Gulf of Mexico north to latitude 32° N'

findings.where: q4-latin view, Latin American independence and US recognition labels; Q4 steps 3-4
findings.what: The labels say 'Mexico 1821', 'Peru 1821', 'Chile 1818'. Is that when the US recognized them? 'Paraguay 1811' is right next to a blue circle, so was Paraguay recognized early? And 'Peru' is written in two places.
findings.why: The year in each label is the independence year, not the recognition date the question asks about. The 'Paraguay 1811' label sits beside the blue circle on Brazil's coast, Paraguay's own orange diamond sits under a big 'Peru' map label, and Brazil's label doesn't show at all. Jordan could list Peru or Paraguay as recognized before 1823.
findings.suggestion: Label each symbol with its recognition year (e.g. 'Buenos Ayres: recognized 1823') or just the name, and place labels right beside their own symbol so Brazil and Paraguay don't swap. I'd also check why the 1800 boundaries layer puts its 'Peru' label east of Bolivia.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png

findings.where: q4-circle view, recognition pop-up; Q4 steps 3-4
